description: Users behind the company reverse proxy occasionally receive another person's admin responses. Both Content-Length and chunked transfer are accepted by different hops.
The login API accepts a JSON body. Sending a non-string password field changes the server's query behaviour and returns a valid session for any username.
A single /api endpoint accepts nested queries describing which fields to return. Asking for the schema documentation still works in production.
A CDN sits in front of the app. After one carefully crafted request, other visitors start seeing pages that include a header value you controlled.
Profile pictures are stored under a URL path the web server serves. Extension checks only look at the final suffix after the last dot.

A note-taking service allocates and frees fixed-size chunks. After free, the next allocation of the same size returns a pointer you partially controlled through an earlier overflow into free metadata.
The binary installs a filter that rejects process creation. File open and read still succeed. Goal is to print the contents of flag.txt.
Only n and e are published. e is almost as large as n. The challenge author mentions the private exponent was chosen unusually small for performance.
Two signatures from the same key are provided. The first component of each signature pair is identical. Recover the private key.
Password-reset tokens look random but consecutive tokens from the same process are enough to predict the next one when the generator is a common stdlib Mersenne Twister.
An online checker compares your guess to the secret with a standard string equality that returns at the first differing character. Network latency is stable enough to measure.
The challenge binary was written in Google's language and stripped. Function names are still recoverable from a large metadata table near the end of the file.
A registration dialog asks for a name and a serial. The serial is not a fixed string; it is derived from the name through several arithmetic transforms inside the binary.
You receive a raw sector dump of a USB stick. The visible filesystem looks empty, but recovery tools that scan unallocated clusters find a deleted text file.
The attachment opens as an image in some tools and as a compressed archive in others. The flag is inside the secondary interpretation.
A Solidity contract exposes a withdraw function marked public. No modifier restricts the caller. Anyone who finds the contract can drain it.
A press photo is the only clue. The camera still embedded coordinates and the editing software name in the file properties.
NX is on and useful pop gadgets are scarce. The C runtime still contains a gadget sequence that loads three argument registers from the stack before calling a function pointer.
Two messages were encrypted with AES in counter mode. The IV field in both packets is the same 16-byte value. XORing the ciphertexts produces readable structure.
Login redirects to an identity provider and back. The return URL parameter is only prefix-checked, so a lookalike domain under your control can receive the authorization code.
The admin API only checks a role field inside a browser-issued token. Changing the algorithm header to none makes the server accept a forged role.
A greeting page echoes your name through a template engine. Entering curly-brace expressions changes the rendered output in ways that look like code evaluation.
The binary prints a user-supplied string with a printf-family call. Feeding percent signs leaks stack values and can write to memory.
Input is copied into a fixed local buffer with gets. Overlong input crashes at a return address you can control.
A long ciphertext was produced by XORing plaintext with a short repeating key. Frequency patterns in the XOR of shifts reveal the key length.
Textbook RSA with exponent three encrypts a short unpadded message. The ciphertext is smaller than the modulus cubed root would require wrapping.
An ordinary-looking PNG is provided. The lowest bit of each color channel carries a hidden bitstream that reconstructs the flag.
A packet capture of HTTP traffic contains a file transfer. Reassembling the TCP stream yields a document with the answer.
The sample's entry point jumps to a stub that unpacks the real code into memory. After the stub runs, the import table is rebuilt.
The challenge text is a long string of letters that looks like base64 but fails to decode until you notice it is hex that was then base64-encoded.
